title: The church sings (Colossians 3:16)
hookLine: the first Christians sang psalms, hymns and spiritual songs

lines: PAUL AND SILAS WEREN'T A ONE-OFF.
cards: A birthday. A stadium. A funeral where nobody can quite hold the note.

When a room sings together, something happens that doesn't happen when one person talks. You may remember Paul and Silas from day eighty-four, singing in the stocks at Philippi while the prisoners listened.
That night wasn't a one-off. Wherever the first Christians turn up, a song is close by. Ever since, in cathedrals, basements and fields, when Christians gather, they sing.

teach.h: THEY SANG AN HYMN, AND WENT OUT.
teach.b: The church sang from its very first night. After the last supper, Mark says, Jesus and his friends sang before walking out: "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives."
Many scholars think it was the psalms Jews sang at Passover, still sung at the Passover table today. So the church's first song was a Jewish song.
Then Paul, writing to the Christians in Colossae, describes their gatherings.

In the King James Bible: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord."
Nobody knows exactly where one kind ends and the next begins.
Psalms likely means the old songs of Israel; hymns, songs of praise; spiritual songs, maybe something newer, even made up in the moment. Notice who teaches whom: one another.
Singing was how they taught. A tune carries words into memory in a way a lecture can't. And outsiders noticed.

teach.h: A ROMAN HEARD THEM BEFORE DAWN.
teach.b: Around the year 112, a Roman governor named Pliny wrote to the emperor that these odd people called Christians met before dawn on a fixed day and sang a hymn to Christ, as to a god.
An official, not a friend, is one of our earliest witnesses that they sang.
Today's line, who sings prays twice, is often credited to Saint Augustine, though scholars can't find those exact words in his writings. He did write about weeping when he heard the church sing.
It stuck because many recognize it: sing a prayer, and your breath and body pray it too.

how: Nearly every Christian church sings when it gathers: Orthodox and many Catholic services chant much of the liturgy, and Protestant congregations sing hymns and worship songs together, often with an organ, piano or band.

o: slow, solemn songs kept for funerals and wakes
newer church songs, maybe made up in the moment
songs sung only by priests, never by the people

games.q: you're a Roman governor around the year 112, writing to the emperor about these odd people called Christians. what do you report they do before dawn?
o: sing a hymn to Christ, as to a god.
games.why: Pliny wrote that they met before dawn on a fixed day and sang a hymn to Christ, as to a god. an outsider, not a friend, is one of our earliest witnesses that they sang.

practice: You don't need a good voice: bring to mind one line of a hymn or church song you know, Amazing grace, Holy, holy, holy, Jesus loves me, or if none come, a tune from a wedding or a funeral.

Breathe in and sing or hum it softly, once, then again slower, noticing where the sound sits in your chest. If you pray, let the line be your prayer; if you don't, just notice what a song does to your breath.

wordCard.voice: Spiritual songs, Paul's third kind of church music, maybe newer, even made up in the moment, alongside psalms and hymns.
